questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (base quantity) with List-II (its SI unit).

List-I:
A. Luminous intensity
B. Amount of substance
C. Thermodynamic temperature
D. Electric current

List-II:
I. kelvin
II. ampere
III. candela
IV. mole

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: The seven SI base quantities and their units
solution.explanation: The SI has seven base units. Four of them are asked here: candela (luminous intensity), mole (amount of substance), kelvin (thermodynamic temperature) and ampere (electric current).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap candela with mole, or kelvin with ampere.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', the international system of units
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The product 4.235 × 2.1, written with the correct number of significant figures, is:

solution.concept: Significant figures in multiplication
solution.explanation: In a product or quotient, the result keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures. 2.1 has two significant figures, so the answer is rounded to two.
steps: Least number of significant figures among the factors = 2 (in 2.1)
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.8935 keeps every calculator digit. 8.89 keeps three significant figures (rounding to decimal places, a rule for addition). 9 keeps only one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', significant figures (rules for arithmetic operations)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A quantity Z is calculated from Z = A²B³/√C. The percentage errors in measuring A, B and C are 1%, 2% and 4% respectively. The maximum percentage error in Z is:

solution.concept: Propagation of relative error through powers
solution.explanation: For Z = (A to the power p)(B to the power q)/(C to the power r), the maximum relative error is p(ΔA/A) + q(ΔB/B) + r(ΔC/C). Errors always add, even for a quantity in the denominator, and each is multiplied by its power.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7% adds the errors without their powers. 12% uses power 1 for C instead of ½. 6% subtracts the error of C because C is in the denominator; maximum errors never subtract.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a new system of units, the unit of mass is 2 kg, the unit of length is 4 m and the unit of time is 2 s. A force of 1 N, expressed in this system, has the numerical value:

solution.concept: Conversion of a numerical value between systems of units
solution.explanation: Force has dimensions [M L T⁻²]. The new unit of force is (2 kg)(4 m)/(2 s)² = 2 N. A force of 1 N is half of this unit. In general n₂ = n₁ (M₁/M₂)(L₁/L₂)(T₁/T₂)⁻².
solution.shortcut: New unit of force = 2 × 4 / 2² = 2 N, so 1 N = 1/2 = 0.5 new unit.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 is the size of the new unit in newtons, not the value of 1 N in the new unit. 8 ignores the time unit. 0.125 ignores the time unit and inverts.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The time period T of small oscillations of a liquid drop is assumed to depend only on the density ρ of the liquid, the radius r of the drop and the surface tension S. By dimensional analysis, T is proportional to:

solution.concept: Finding a relation by the method of dimensions
solution.explanation: Write T = k ρᵃ rᵇ Sᶜ and equate the powers of M, L and T on both sides. Surface tension is force per length, [M T⁻²], and density is [M L⁻³].
solution.why_others_wrong: √(S/(ρr³)) is the inverse (it has the dimensions of frequency). √(ρr²/S) and √(ρr/S) do not have the dimensions of time: their L powers do not cancel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensional analysis and its applications

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two resistors of resistances R₁ = (30 ± 0.9) Ω and R₂ = (60 ± 1.8) Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance, with its maximum absolute error, is:

solution.concept: Error in a quantity given by a reciprocal sum
solution.explanation: For 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, differentiating gives ΔR/R² = ΔR₁/R₁² + ΔR₂/R₂² for the maximum error.
solution.why_others_wrong: (20.0 ± 1.2) Ω adds the relative errors (3% + 3%) as for a product. (20.0 ± 2.7) Ω adds the absolute errors as for a sum. (90.0 ± 2.7) Ω treats the resistors as in series.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car starts from rest and moves along a straight road with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s². The distance it covers in the first 5 s is:

solution.concept: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion
solution.explanation: With u = 0, the distance covered in time t is s = ½at².
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 m drops the ½. 10 m is the final velocity (in m/s), not a distance. 100 m squares the product at.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (feature of a motion graph) with List-II (what it gives).

List-I:
A. Slope of a position–time graph
B. Slope of a velocity–time graph
C. Area under a velocity–time graph
D. Area under an acceleration–time graph

List-II:
I. Change in velocity
II. Displacement
III. Velocity
IV. Acceleration

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Reading slopes and areas of kinematic graphs
solution.explanation: A slope is a rate of change: dx/dt = v and dv/dt = a. An area is an accumulation: ∫v dt = displacement and ∫a dt = change in velocity.
steps: Slope of x–t = dx/dt = velocity → III
Slope of v–t = dv/dt = acceleration → IV
Area under v–t = ∫v dt = displacement → II
Area under a–t = ∫a dt = change in velocity → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap slope and area, or confuse velocity with acceleration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', instantaneous velocity and acceleration
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about vectors are correct?

(a) The scalar (dot) product of two vectors is commutative: A·B = B·A.
(b) The vector (cross) product of two vectors is commutative: A × B = B × A.
(c) î × ĵ = k̂ for the unit vectors of a right-handed coordinate system.
(d) The scalar product of two perpendicular vectors is zero.
(e) Two vectors of unequal magnitudes can add up to give a zero resultant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Properties of scalar and vector products
solution.explanation: A·B = AB cos θ is the same either way round, and is zero when θ = 90°. The cross product changes sign when the order is reversed: B × A = −(A × B). Two vectors can cancel only if they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
steps: (a) True: AB cos θ is symmetric
(e) False: |A + B| ≥ |A| − |B| > 0 when the magnitudes differ
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', scalars and vectors (scalar and vector products)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: For a projectile moving under gravity alone (air resistance neglected), which of the following remains constant throughout its flight?

options.text: The vertical component of its velocity
The horizontal component of its velocity

solution.concept: Independence of horizontal and vertical motion
solution.explanation: Gravity acts vertically, so there is no horizontal acceleration. The horizontal velocity u cos θ stays the same, while the vertical velocity changes at the rate g.
steps: aₓ = 0 → vₓ = u cos θ throughout
a_y = −g → v_y = u sin θ − gt changes
Speed and kinetic energy depend on v_y, so they change too
solution.why_others_wrong: Speed and kinetic energy are least at the top and greatest at launch and landing. The vertical component decreases, becomes zero at the top, then grows downward.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion
solution.final_answer: Option C: The horizontal component of its velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Rain is falling vertically downward with a speed of 12 m/s. A woman runs along a horizontal road with a speed of 5 m/s. The speed of the rain relative to the woman is:

solution.concept: Relative velocity in two dimensions
solution.explanation: Velocity of rain relative to the woman = v_rain − v_woman. The two velocities are perpendicular, so the relative velocity has components 12 m/s (down) and 5 m/s (opposite to her motion).
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 m/s adds the speeds and 7 m/s subtracts them, as if the velocities were along one line. 12 m/s ignores the woman's motion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A stone is dropped from rest from the top of a tower 80 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the distance it falls during the last second of its fall is:

solution.concept: Free fall: distance in a particular second
solution.explanation: First find the total time of fall, then subtract the distance covered up to one second before landing.
steps: Time of fall: 80 = ½ × 10 × t² → t = 4 s
Distance in first 3 s = ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m
Distance in the last (4th) second = 80 − 45 = 35 m
solution.shortcut: Distance in the nth second from rest = (g/2)(2n − 1) = 5 × 7 = 35 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 45 m is the distance in the first 3 s. 20 m is the average distance per second (80/4). 40 m is the speed (in m/s) on reaching the ground.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about motion in a straight line are correct?

(a) A body can have zero velocity and a non-zero acceleration at the same instant.
(b) Over any time interval, the average speed is greater than or equal to the magnitude of the average velocity.
(c) If the acceleration is opposite in direction to the velocity, the speed of the body decreases.
(d) A body whose velocity–time graph is a straight line with a negative slope is always slowing down.
(e) If the distance travelled by a body is non-zero, its displacement cannot be zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Speed, velocity and acceleration
solution.explanation: A ball thrown upward has v = 0 but a = g at the top. Distance is never less than the magnitude of displacement, so average speed ≥ |average velocity|. Acceleration opposite to velocity slows the body. A straight v–t line with negative slope means constant negative acceleration: the body slows only while v is positive, then speeds up in the negative direction. A round trip has non-zero distance but zero displacement.
steps: (a) True: top of a vertical throw
(d) False: after v passes through zero, v and a point the same way and the speed increases
(e) False: a round trip has zero displacement
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', average velocity and average speed; acceleration

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is thrown horizontally with a speed of 20 m/s from the top of a cliff 45 m high. Taking g = 10 m/s², how far from the foot of the cliff does it hit the level ground below?

solution.concept: Horizontal projection
solution.explanation: The time of fall depends only on the height (vertical motion from rest). During that time the ball moves horizontally at a constant 20 m/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 42.4 m uses t = √(h/g), forgetting the 2. 120 m doubles the time as if the ball also had to rise first. 45 m just equates the horizontal distance with the height.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In uniform circular motion, the acceleration of the particle is constant.
Reason (R): In uniform circular motion, the speed of the particle is constant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion
solution.explanation: The magnitude of the acceleration, v²/R, is constant, but its direction keeps changing so that it always points towards the centre. A vector whose direction changes is not constant, so A is false. The speed is constant by definition of uniform circular motion, so R is true.
steps: Acceleration = v²/R towards the centre; its direction rotates with the particle → not a constant vector
Speed is constant → R is true
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A and B need A to be true. Option C has R false, but constant speed is what 'uniform' means.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', uniform circular motion
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle is projected from level ground with a speed of 10√3 m/s at an angle of 60° above the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², after how much time does its velocity become perpendicular to its initial velocity?

solution.concept: Velocity of a projectile as a vector; perpendicular vectors have zero dot product
solution.explanation: Write the velocity at time t in components and set its dot product with the initial velocity to zero. Then check that this time is before the particle lands.
steps: Time of flight = 2u_y/g = 3 s, so t = 2 s is during the flight
solution.shortcut: u · v = u² − g t u sin θ = 0 → t = u/(g sin θ) = 10√3/(10 × √3/2) = 2 s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 s is the time of flight. 1.5 s is the time to reach the top, where velocity is horizontal, not perpendicular to the initial velocity. √3 s is u/g, which drops the sin θ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A river 120 m wide flows at 3 m/s. A swimmer can swim at 5 m/s relative to still water. If she wants to reach the point directly opposite her starting point, the time she takes to cross is:

solution.concept: Crossing a river along the shortest path
solution.explanation: To go straight across, she must head partly upstream so that the upstream component of her velocity cancels the river's 3 m/s. Only the remaining component carries her across.
steps: Upstream component = 3 m/s → cross-stream component = √(5² − 3²) = 4 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 s (120/5) is the shortest-time crossing, heading straight across and drifting downstream. 40 s divides by the river speed. 15 s divides by the sum of the speeds.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The position of a particle moving along the x-axis is x = t³ − 6t² + 9t, where x is in metres and t in seconds. The distance travelled by the particle from t = 0 to t = 3 s is:

solution.concept: Distance versus displacement when the particle turns back
solution.explanation: Distance must be found leg by leg: find where the velocity is zero (turning points), then add the magnitudes of the displacements of each leg.
steps: v = dx/dt = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) → turns at t = 1 s
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 m is the displacement. 4 m counts only the first leg. 16 m counts each leg twice.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For projectiles launched from level ground with the same speed, the horizontal range is the same for angles of projection 15° and 75°.
Statement II: For projectiles launched from level ground with the same speed, the time of flight does not depend on the angle of projection.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Range and time of flight of a projectile
solution.explanation: R = u² sin 2θ/g, and sin 30° = sin 150°, so complementary angles give equal ranges: Statement I is true. T = 2u sin θ/g depends on θ (the 75° projectile stays in the air longer), so Statement II is false.
steps: R(15°) ∝ sin 30° = ½; R(75°) ∝ sin 150° = ½ → equal → I true
T ∝ sin θ: sin 75° > sin 15° → different times → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', projectile motion
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball of mass 200 g moving horizontally at 10 m/s strikes a vertical wall and rebounds along the same line with the same speed. The magnitude of the impulse delivered to the ball by the wall is:

solution.concept: Impulse equals change in momentum
solution.explanation: Momentum is a vector. When the ball reverses direction, the change in velocity is 10 − (−10) = 20 m/s, not zero.
steps: Take the rebound direction as positive: initial p = 0.2 × (−10) = −2 kg m/s, final p = +2 kg m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 N s counts only stopping the ball, not sending it back. 0 N s treats momentum as a scalar because the speed is unchanged. 20 N s forgets to multiply the change in velocity by the mass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Passengers standing in a bus tend to fall backward when the bus suddenly starts moving forward. This is best explained by:

solution.concept: Newton's first law: inertia
solution.explanation: The bus floor drags the feet forward, but the upper body, having no forward force on it at first, tends to stay at rest. Relative to the bus, the passenger falls backward.
steps: Upper body tends to remain at rest (inertia of rest)
Relative to the accelerating bus, the body tilts backward
solution.why_others_wrong: Inertia of direction explains being thrown sideways on a turn. Newton's third law concerns action–reaction pairs, and energy conservation does not explain this tendency.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's first law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A gun recoils backward when a bullet is fired from it.
Reason (R): When no external horizontal force acts on the gun–bullet system, its total linear momentum is conserved, and it is zero before firing.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Conservation of linear momentum
solution.explanation: Before firing, the gun and bullet are at rest, so the total momentum is zero. After firing, the bullet's forward momentum must be balanced by an equal backward momentum of the gun. R is true and is exactly why the gun recoils.
steps: Final: m_b v_b + M v_g = 0 → v_g = −m_b v_b / M (backward)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text: A curved road of radius 40 m is banked at 45°. Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed at which a car can take this turn without needing any friction is:

solution.concept: Optimum speed on a banked road
solution.explanation: At this speed the horizontal component of the normal reaction alone provides the centripetal force: N sin θ = mv²/r and N cos θ = mg, so v² = rg tan θ.
steps: v² = r g tan θ = 40 × 10 × tan 45° = 400
solution.why_others_wrong: 400 m/s forgets the square root. 16.8 m/s uses sin θ in place of tan θ. 28.3 m/s uses v² = 2rg, mixing in a free-fall formula.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', motion of a car on a banked road

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 5 kg block rests on a horizontal floor. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction between them are 0.4 and 0.25. A horizontal force of 15 N is applied to the block. Taking g = 10 m/s², the friction force on the block is:

solution.concept: Static friction is self-adjusting
solution.explanation: First check whether the block moves. The largest static friction possible is μₛN = 20 N. The applied 15 N is less than this, so the block stays at rest and static friction just balances the applied force.
steps: N = mg = 50 N; limiting friction = 0.4 × 50 = 20 N
Applied force 15 N < 20 N → no motion
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 N is the limiting (maximum) value, reached only when the block is about to slip. 12.5 N is kinetic friction, which acts only once the block slides. 0 N ignores friction altogether.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two blocks of masses 3 kg and 2 kg are in contact on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal force of 10 N is applied to the 3 kg block, pushing both blocks together. The force exerted by the 3 kg block on the 2 kg block is:

solution.concept: Newton's second law applied to a system and to one part of it
solution.explanation: Both blocks share the same acceleration. The only horizontal force on the 2 kg block is the contact force, so it must equal (2 kg) × a.
steps: 2 kg block alone: contact force = 2 × 2 = 4 N
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 N is the net force on the 3 kg block, not the contact force. 10 N assumes the full applied force is passed on. 2 N is the acceleration in m/s².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion: level and banked roads
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (body moving in a circle) with List-II (force that provides the centripetal force).

List-I:
A. A car taking a turn on a level (unbanked) road
B. A satellite in a circular orbit around the Earth
C. A stone whirled in a horizontal circle at the end of a string
D. An electron revolving around the nucleus in Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom

List-II:
I. Gravitational force
II. Tension
III. Friction
IV. Electrostatic attraction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Centripetal force is supplied by a real force
solution.explanation: Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; in each case some real force points towards the centre.
steps: Car on a level road: static friction between tyres and road → III
Stone on a string: tension in the string → II
Electron in Bohr's model: Coulomb attraction of the nucleus → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap friction with tension, or gravity with the electrostatic force.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', dynamics of uniform circular motion
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Three forces of magnitudes 3 N, 4 N and 8 N, acting at a point, can keep a particle in equilibrium.
Statement II: A particle acted on by concurrent forces is in equilibrium only if the vector sum of the forces is zero.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Equilibrium of concurrent forces
solution.explanation: For equilibrium the forces must form a closed triangle, so the largest force cannot exceed the sum of the other two. The resultant of 3 N and 4 N lies between 1 N and 7 N, so it can never balance 8 N: Statement I is false. Statement II is the condition for equilibrium: true.
steps: Resultant of 3 N and 4 N: 1 N ≤ R ≤ 7 N
8 N > 7 N → cannot be balanced → I false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): It is easier to pull a lawn roller by a handle inclined above the horizontal than to push it with the same handle.
Reason (R): While pulling, the vertical component of the applied force acts upward and reduces the normal reaction, and hence the friction force; while pushing, it acts downward and increases them.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Friction depends on the normal reaction
solution.explanation: Friction is proportional to the normal reaction. Pulling at an angle θ gives N = mg − F sin θ; pushing gives N = mg + F sin θ. Less normal reaction means less friction to overcome, so pulling is easier. R is true and explains A.
steps: Pull: N = mg − F sin θ → smaller friction
Push: N = mg + F sin θ → larger friction
R gives the reason for A
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block slides down a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is 1/(2√3). Taking g = 10 m/s², the acceleration of the block is:

solution.concept: Motion on a rough inclined plane
solution.explanation: Along the incline, the gravity component mg sin θ pulls the block down and kinetic friction μₖmg cos θ acts up the incline (opposing the sliding).
steps: a = g(sin θ − μₖ cos θ)
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.0 m/s² ignores friction. 7.5 m/s² adds friction as if it helped the motion. 3.6 m/s² takes friction as μₖ mg sin θ instead of μₖ mg cos θ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A shell of mass 4 kg at rest explodes into three pieces. Two pieces, each of mass 1 kg, fly off perpendicular to each other, each with a speed of 30 m/s. The speed of the third piece is:

solution.concept: Conservation of linear momentum in two dimensions
solution.explanation: The total momentum is zero before and after the explosion. So the third piece (mass 4 − 1 − 1 = 2 kg) must carry momentum equal and opposite to the vector sum of the other two.
steps: Momentum of each 1 kg piece = 30 kg m/s, at right angles
Third piece: 2 × v = 30√2 → v = 15√2 m/s ≈ 21.2 m/s
solution.why_others_wrong: 30√2 m/s forgets to divide by the 2 kg mass of the third piece. 30 m/s adds the momenta as scalars (60/2). 10√2 m/s divides by 3 kg instead of the 2 kg mass of the third piece.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two blocks of masses 3 kg and 5 kg hang at the two ends of a light inextensible string passing over a smooth, light pulley. The system is released from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string is:

solution.concept: Newton's second law for connected bodies
solution.explanation: The heavier block accelerates down and the lighter one up with the same acceleration a. Write F = ma for each block separately and solve for T.
steps: For the 3 kg block: T − 30 = 3 × 2.5 → T = 37.5 N
Check with the 5 kg block: 50 − T = 5 × 2.5 → T = 37.5 N
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 N and 50 N are the weights of the blocks; the tension lies between them because both blocks accelerate. 20 N is the net driving force (m₂ − m₁)g.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about friction are correct?

(a) Static friction is self-adjusting: it takes any value up to a limiting value.
(b) For a given pair of surfaces, the coefficient of kinetic friction is generally less than the coefficient of static friction.
(c) For the same normal reaction, limiting friction increases with the area of contact.
(d) Kinetic friction acts opposite to the velocity of a body relative to the surface it slides on.
(e) Rolling friction is generally much smaller than sliding friction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Laws of friction
solution.explanation: Static friction matches the applied force up to μₛN; once sliding starts, μₖ (usually smaller than μₛ) applies. Limiting friction depends on the normal reaction, not on the area of contact. Friction opposes relative motion. Rolling friction is much smaller, which is why wheels and ball bearings help.
steps: (c) False: independent of area of contact
(d) True: kinetic friction opposes relative velocity
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (c), the area trap, or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction (static, kinetic and rolling friction)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle with constant speed. The work done by the tension in the string during one complete revolution is:

options.text: Equal to the kinetic energy of the stone

solution.concept: Work done by a force perpendicular to displacement
solution.explanation: In uniform circular motion the tension points towards the centre, while each small displacement is along the tangent. Since F ⊥ ds at every instant, W = ∫F·ds = 0. This agrees with the work-energy theorem: the speed, and so the kinetic energy, does not change.
steps: W = 0 for every part of the circle
solution.why_others_wrong: A force always at 90° to the motion can change the direction of the velocity but not the speed, so it does no work, neither positive nor negative.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the scalar product and work

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is compressed by 10 cm from its natural length. The potential energy stored in the spring is:

solution.concept: Elastic potential energy of a spring
solution.explanation: The work done in compressing the spring against the force kx is stored as U = ½kx².
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 J drops the ½. 20 J is the spring force kx (in newtons), not energy. 10 J uses ½kx instead of ½kx².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Power is the rate at which work is done, and its SI unit is the watt.
Statement II: One kilowatt hour (kWh) is equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Power and the commercial unit of energy
solution.explanation: P = dW/dt, measured in J/s = W, so Statement I is true. 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, so Statement II is true. The kWh is a unit of energy, not of power.
steps: P = W/t → watt (J s⁻¹) → I true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (type of collision) with List-II (its feature). All collisions are head-on, in one dimension.

List-I:
A. Perfectly elastic collision
B. Perfectly inelastic collision
C. Elastic collision of two equal masses, one initially at rest
D. Elastic collision of a very light body with a very heavy body at rest

List-II:
I. The velocities of the two bodies are exchanged
II. The light body rebounds with nearly its original speed
III. The bodies move together after the collision
IV. The total kinetic energy after the collision equals that before it

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Elastic and inelastic collisions in one dimension
solution.explanation: In every collision momentum is conserved. In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is also the same before and after. In a perfectly inelastic one the bodies stick together. The elastic results v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂) and v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂) give the two special cases.
steps: Perfectly elastic: KE after = KE before → IV
Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick and move together → III
m₁ = m₂: v₁ = 0, v₂ = u → velocities exchanged → I
m₁ ≪ m₂: v₁ ≈ −u, v₂ ≈ 0 → light body rebounds with nearly the same speed → II
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the two general cases (IV and III) or the two special cases (I and II).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions in one dimension
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: A force F = 3x² N, where x is in metres, acts on a particle along the x-axis. The work done by this force as the particle moves from x = 0 to x = 2 m is:

solution.concept: Work done by a variable force
solution.explanation: When the force changes with position, the work is the area under the F–x curve: W = ∫F dx.
solution.why_others_wrong: 24 J multiplies the final force (12 N) by the displacement, as if the force were constant. 12 J uses the average of the end forces, which works only for a force linear in x. 2.67 J integrates x² but drops the factor 3.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The work done by friction on a body can be positive.
Reason (R): Friction always opposes the motion of a body.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Friction opposes relative motion, not motion
solution.explanation: A box on the floor of a truck that is speeding up is carried forward by static friction from the floor. That friction acts along the box's displacement, so it does positive work and increases the box's kinetic energy: A is true. Friction opposes relative motion between the surfaces, not the motion of the body itself, so R is false.
steps: Box on an accelerating truck: friction forward, displacement forward → W > 0 → A true
Friction opposes relative motion (slipping), not motion as such → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A and B need R to be true. Option D is wrong because A is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small stone tied to a light string of length 1.6 m is whirled in a vertical circle. Taking g = 10 m/s², the minimum speed it must have at the lowest point to just complete the circle is:

solution.concept: Minimum speed in a vertical circle (string)
solution.explanation: A string can only pull. At the top the string just goes slack when gravity alone provides the centripetal force: v_top² = gr. Energy conservation from the bottom to the top (a rise of 2r) then gives v_bottom.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 m/s is the minimum speed at the top, √(gr). 4√2 m/s is √(2gr). 8 m/s is √(4gr), which is right for a rigid rod (it can push, so the speed at the top may be zero) but not for a string.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', motion in a vertical circle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass 2 kg moving at 6 m/s collides head-on and elastically with a body of mass 4 kg at rest. The fraction of the initial kinetic energy transferred to the 4 kg body is:

solution.concept: Elastic collision in one dimension
solution.explanation: Use the elastic-collision results for a target at rest to find the velocity of the 4 kg body, then compare kinetic energies.
steps: KE given to the 4 kg body = ½ × 4 × 4² = 32 J; initial KE = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/9 is the fraction kept by the 2 kg body. 2/3 is the velocity ratio v₂/u. 4/9 squares the velocity ratio but ignores the different masses.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A bullet of mass 10 g moving horizontally at 200 m/s gets embedded in a wooden block of mass 990 g suspended by a long string. Taking g = 10 m/s², the maximum height through which the block (with the bullet) rises is:

solution.concept: Perfectly inelastic collision followed by energy conservation
solution.explanation: Two stages. During the collision only momentum is conserved (kinetic energy is lost as heat). After the collision, mechanical energy is conserved as the block swings up.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 m wrongly conserves kinetic energy through the collision (200 J = 1 kg × 10 × h). 0.4 m uses h = V²/g. 0.1 m uses h = V²/4g.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In an elastic collision, the total kinetic energy is conserved at every instant during the collision.
(b) Total linear momentum of an isolated system is conserved in both elastic and inelastic collisions.
(c) The work done by a conservative force on a body moving around a closed path is zero.
(d) The total mechanical energy of a body sliding on a rough surface remains constant.
(e) In an inelastic collision, part of the initial kinetic energy is converted into other forms such as heat, sound and energy of deformation.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Momentum, kinetic energy and conservative forces
solution.explanation: During any collision the bodies deform and some kinetic energy is temporarily stored; only in the elastic case is the total after the collision equal to that before. Momentum is conserved in all collisions of an isolated system. Friction is non-conservative, so it reduces mechanical energy.
steps: (a) False: KE is not conserved during the short time of deformation
(c) True: definition of a conservative force
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (a) miss the 'during the collision' trap; the option with (d) ignores that friction is non-conservative.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', conservative forces and collisions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two particles of masses 2 kg and 3 kg are placed on the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 5 m respectively. The position of their centre of mass is:

solution.concept: Centre of mass of a two-particle system
solution.explanation: X = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂)/(m₁ + m₂). The centre of mass lies closer to the heavier particle.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 m is the distance from the heavier particle, i.e. the masses were swapped. 2.5 m is the midpoint, right only for equal masses. 7.5 m divides by 2 kg alone instead of the total mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of mass

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (quantity in linear motion) with List-II (its analogue in rotational motion).

List-I:
A. Mass
B. Force
C. Linear momentum
D. Linear velocity

List-II:
I. Torque
II. Angular momentum
III. Moment of inertia
IV. Angular velocity

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Comparison of translational and rotational motion
solution.explanation: Every translational quantity has a rotational analogue: F = ma corresponds to τ = Iα, p = mv to L = Iω.
steps: Mass m ↔ moment of inertia I → III
Linear momentum p ↔ angular momentum L → II
Velocity v ↔ angular velocity ω → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap force with mass, or momentum with force, which breaks F = ma ↔ τ = Iα.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', comparison of translational and rotational motion
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: The moment of inertia of a rigid body about a given axis does NOT depend on:

options.text: How the mass is distributed about the axis
The position and orientation of the axis
The angular velocity of the body

solution.concept: What moment of inertia depends on
solution.explanation: I = Σmᵢrᵢ², where rᵢ is the perpendicular distance of each particle from the axis. It depends on the masses and their distances from the chosen axis, but not on how fast the body is rotating.
steps: Depends on mass, its distribution and the axis
ω does not appear → independent of ω
solution.why_others_wrong: Mass, mass distribution and the choice of axis all enter Σmᵢrᵢ² directly.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia
solution.final_answer: Option D: The angular velocity of the body

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A diver pulls in her arms and legs during a somersault to spin faster.
Reason (R): When no external torque acts, angular momentum Iω is conserved, so reducing the moment of inertia increases the angular speed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum
solution.explanation: Gravity acts at the centre of mass, so it gives no torque about it: angular momentum about the centre of mass stays constant. Tucking in brings mass closer to the axis, I falls and ω rises. R is true and explains A.
steps: No external torque about the centre of mass → Iω = constant
Tuck in → I decreases → ω increases
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', conservation of angular momentum
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (body of mass M) with List-II (its moment of inertia about the stated axis).

List-I:
A. Thin rod of length L, about an axis perpendicular to it through its centre
B. Thin circular ring of radius R, about a diameter
C. Uniform circular disc of radius R, about a diameter
D. Uniform solid sphere of radius R, about a diameter

List-II:
I. MR²/4
II. 2MR²/5
III. ML²/12
IV. MR²/2

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Moments of inertia of standard bodies
solution.explanation: For the ring and the disc, the diameter values follow from the perpendicular axis theorem: the moment of inertia about the central axis normal to the plane (MR² for a ring, MR²/2 for a disc) equals the sum of the moments about two perpendicular diameters.
steps: Rod about its centre: ML²/12 → III
Ring about a diameter: MR²/2 (half of MR²) → IV
Disc about a diameter: MR²/4 (half of MR²/2) → I
Solid sphere about a diameter: 2MR²/5 → II
solution.why_others_wrong: The usual slips are swapping the ring and disc values, or taking the sphere as MR²/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia (table of simple bodies)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A disc rotates freely about a fixed vertical axis through its centre with angular velocity ω. An identical disc, initially not rotating, is gently placed on it coaxially, and the two soon rotate together. The fraction of the initial rotational kinetic energy that is lost is:

solution.concept: Conservation of angular momentum with loss of kinetic energy
solution.explanation: There is no external torque about the axis, so angular momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy is not conserved: friction between the discs, which brings them to a common speed, turns some of it into heat.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3/4 takes the final kinetic energy as ½Iω'² with the original I, forgetting the doubled moment of inertia. 0 wrongly assumes kinetic energy is conserved. 1/4 reports the final energy as a fraction of Iω², not the fraction lost.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a rigid body rotates about a fixed axis, all its particles have the same linear speed.
Statement II: When a rigid body rotates about a fixed axis, all its particles have the same angular velocity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Kinematics of rotation about a fixed axis
solution.explanation: Each particle moves in a circle centred on the axis, and the whole body turns through the same angle in the same time, so ω is common: Statement II is true. Linear speed v = ωr grows with distance r from the axis, so Statement I is false.
steps: v = ωr → particles farther from the axis move faster → I false
Same ω for all particles → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular velocity and its relation with linear velocity
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A light string is wound round the rim of a uniform disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m, which can rotate freely about a fixed horizontal axis through its centre. The string is pulled with a constant force of 10 N. The angular acceleration of the disc is:

solution.concept: Torque and angular acceleration: τ = Iα
solution.explanation: The string pulls tangentially at the rim, so the torque is F × R. A uniform disc about its central axis has I = ½MR².
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 rad/s² uses I = MR² (a ring). 20 rad/s² takes the torque as just F = 10, without the lever arm R. 2.5 rad/s² is F/M, a linear acceleration, not an angular one.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium only if both the net external force and the net external torque on it are zero.
Statement II: A couple (two equal and opposite forces with different lines of action) produces translation of a body without rotation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Conditions of equilibrium; the couple
solution.explanation: Zero net force gives translational equilibrium, zero net torque gives rotational equilibrium; both are needed, so Statement I is true. A couple has zero net force (no translation) but a non-zero torque, so it produces rotation without translation: Statement II is false.
steps: Equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 → I true
Couple: ΣF = 0 but τ ≠ 0 → rotation only → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', equilibrium of a rigid body; couple
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: A uniform disc has mass 2 kg and radius 20 cm. Its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to its plane and passing through a point on its rim is:

solution.concept: Theorem of parallel axes
solution.explanation: Start from the axis through the centre perpendicular to the plane (I = ½MR²) and shift it parallel by R to the rim: I = I_cm + MR².
steps: Parallel axis at distance R: I = 0.04 + 2 × 0.2² = 0.04 + 0.08
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.04 kg m² is the value about the central axis. 0.16 kg m² uses MR² for the central axis (a ring). 0.10 kg m² starts from the diameter value MR²/4, but the required axis is parallel to the central perpendicular axis, not to a diameter.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform beam 4 m long and of mass 20 kg rests horizontally on two supports at its ends. A load of mass 40 kg is placed on it 1 m from the left end. Taking g = 10 m/s², the reaction force at the left support is:

solution.concept: Rotational and translational equilibrium
solution.explanation: Take moments about the right support, so its unknown reaction drops out. The beam's weight acts at its centre (2 m from either end) and the load is 3 m from the right end.
steps: Moments about the right end: R_L × 4 = 200 × 2 + 400 × 3 = 1600
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 N is the reaction at the right support. 300 N shares the total weight equally, ignoring where the load is. 600 N puts the whole weight on one support.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle of mass 2 kg moves with a constant velocity of 4 m/s along the line y = 3 m in the x–y plane, parallel to the x-axis. The magnitude of its angular momentum about the origin is:

solution.concept: Angular momentum of a particle moving in a straight line
solution.explanation: L = r × p. Its magnitude is p times the perpendicular distance of the line of motion from the origin, which is 3 m for every position on the line. So L is constant even though the particle moves in a straight line.
steps: Perpendicular distance of the line y = 3 m from the origin = 3 m
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 assumes a particle moving in a straight line has no angular momentum; that is true only about points on its line of motion. 12 kg m²/s forgets the mass. 8 kg m²/s is the linear momentum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The centre of mass of a body may lie at a point where there is no mass of the body.
(b) The centre of mass of a system moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all the external forces acted there.
(c) Internal forces between the particles of a system can change the velocity of its centre of mass.
(d) For the same mass and radius, a thin ring has a greater moment of inertia than a uniform disc about their central axes perpendicular to their planes.
(e) If the net external force on a system is zero, its centre of mass must be at rest.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Motion of the centre of mass; distribution of mass
solution.explanation: The centre of mass of a ring is at its centre, where there is no material. Internal forces cancel in pairs (Newton's third law), so only external forces change the motion of the centre of mass. With zero external force the centre of mass moves with constant velocity, which need not be zero. A ring has all its mass at distance R (MR²), a disc has much of it nearer the axis (MR²/2).
steps: (c) False: internal forces cancel in pairs
(e) False: v_cm is constant, not necessarily zero
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', motion of centre of mass

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the gravitational force between two point masses are correct?

(a) It is always attractive.
(b) It varies inversely as the square of the distance between the masses.
(c) It depends on the medium between the masses.
(d) It acts along the line joining the two masses.
(e) The value of the universal gravitational constant G is different at different places on the Earth.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Newton's law of universal gravitation
solution.explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r², directed along the line joining the masses and always attractive. G is a universal constant, and unlike the electrostatic force, gravitation does not depend on the medium in between.
steps: (c) False: independent of the intervening medium
(e) False: G is universal; it is g that varies
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', universal law of gravitation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The escape speed from the Earth's surface is 11.2 km/s. A planet has 8 times the mass and 2 times the radius of the Earth. The escape speed from its surface is:

solution.concept: Escape speed v_e = √(2GM/R)
solution.explanation: Escape speed varies as √(M/R). Here M/R becomes 8/2 = 4 times, so v_e becomes √4 = 2 times.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.2 km/s ignores the change in mass and radius. 44.8 km/s forgets the square root. 5.6 km/s inverts the ratio.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (law) with List-II (its statement).

List-I:
A. Kepler's first law
B. Kepler's second law
C. Kepler's third law
D. Newton's law of gravitation

List-II:
I. The square of the period of revolution is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis
II. The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time
III. Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus
IV. F = Gm₁m₂/r²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Kepler's laws of planetary motion
solution.explanation: First law: law of orbits. Second law: law of areas. Third law: law of periods.
steps: First law (orbits): ellipse with the Sun at a focus → III
Second law (areas): equal areas in equal times → II
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the first and second laws, or the second and third.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', Kepler's laws
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A planet moves round the Sun in a nearly circular orbit whose radius is 4 times the radius of the Earth's orbit. Its period of revolution is:

solution.concept: Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³
solution.explanation: Compare with the Earth (T = 1 year): T_p/T_E = (r_p/r_E)^(3/2).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 years assumes T ∝ r. 16 years uses T ∝ r². 2 years uses T ∝ √r.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A satellite revolves in a circular orbit at a height above the Earth's surface equal to the Earth's radius. Taking the Earth's radius as 6400 km and g = 10 m/s² at the surface, the orbital speed of the satellite is about:

solution.concept: Orbital speed v = √(GM/r)
solution.explanation: The orbit radius is r = R + h = 2R. Use GM = gR² to avoid needing G and M.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.0 km/s is the orbital speed close to the surface (r = R). 11.3 km/s is the escape speed √(2gR). 4.0 km/s halves √(gR) instead of dividing gR by 2 under the root.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body of mass m is raised from the surface of the Earth to a height equal to the Earth's radius R. If g is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface, the work done against gravity is:

solution.concept: Gravitational potential energy U = −GMm/r
solution.explanation: For heights comparable to R, g is not constant, so mgh does not apply. Use the change in U = −GMm/r with GM = gR².
solution.why_others_wrong: mgR uses mgh with g taken as constant. mgR/4 uses the value of g at height R (g/4) throughout. 5mgR/8 averages the values of g at the two ends, which is still not the correct integral.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The period of a satellite in a circular orbit close to the Earth's surface depends on the mass of the satellite.
Statement II: Assuming the Earth to be a sphere of uniform density, the acceleration due to gravity decreases as one goes below the Earth's surface.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Satellite period; g at depth
solution.explanation: T = 2π√(r³/GM) contains only the Earth's mass, not the satellite's, so Statement I is false. Below the surface g(d) = g(1 − d/R), which decreases with depth, so Statement II is true.
steps: T = 2π√(r³/GM): no satellite mass → I false
g(d) = g(1 − d/R) → decreases → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity below the surface; earth satellites
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A satellite of mass m is moved from a circular orbit of radius 2R to a circular orbit of radius 4R around the Earth, where R is the Earth's radius. If g is the acceleration due to gravity at the Earth's surface, the minimum energy that must be supplied is:

solution.concept: Total energy of a satellite: E = −GMm/2r
solution.explanation: The energy to be supplied is the increase in total (kinetic + potential) energy, not just in potential energy, because the satellite also slows down in the higher orbit.
solution.why_others_wrong: mgR/4 is the change in potential energy alone; the kinetic energy decreases by mgR/8 and offsets half of it. mgR/15 treats 2R and 4R as heights above the surface (radii 3R and 5R). 3mgR/8 adds the magnitudes of the two energies instead of subtracting.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body is projected vertically upward from the Earth's surface with a speed equal to half the escape speed. If R is the radius of the Earth, the maximum height it reaches above the surface is (neglect air resistance):

solution.concept: Energy conservation in a non-uniform gravitational field
solution.explanation: g falls off with height, so use energy conservation with U = −GMm/r, not v² = 2gh.
solution.why_others_wrong: R/4 uses h = v²/2g with constant g. R drops the ½ in the kinetic energy. R/7 takes the escape speed as √(gR) instead of √(2gR).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): An astronaut inside a satellite orbiting the Earth experiences weightlessness.
Reason (R): The gravitational force of the Earth on the astronaut in orbit is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Weightlessness in orbit
solution.explanation: The astronaut and the satellite both fall freely towards the Earth with the same acceleration, so the floor pushes on the astronaut with zero force: A is true. Gravity at orbital heights is still strong (it is what keeps the satellite in orbit), so R is false.
steps: Both in free fall with the same acceleration → no normal reaction → weightless → A true
Gravity provides the centripetal force of the orbit, so it is not zero → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options A and B accept the false reason. Option D denies the true assertion.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steel wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm² hangs from a rigid support and carries a load of mass 10 kg. Young's modulus of steel is 2 × 10¹¹ N/m² and g = 10 m/s². The extension of the wire is:

solution.concept: Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L)
solution.explanation: Rearrange Young's modulus for the extension, ΔL = FL/(AY), and work in SI units: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m².
steps: F = mg = 100 N; A = 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 mm uses the mass (10) instead of the weight (100 N). 1 m converts 1 mm² to 10⁻⁹ m². 0.01 mm converts 1 mm² to 10⁻⁴ m².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a hydraulic lift, the small piston has a radius of 2 cm and the large piston a radius of 10 cm. A force of 200 N is applied on the small piston. The largest load the large piston can support is:

solution.concept: Pascal's law: pressure is transmitted undiminished
solution.explanation: The same pressure acts on both pistons, so F₂/A₂ = F₁/A₁. The force is multiplied by the ratio of areas, which is the square of the ratio of radii.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1000 N uses the ratio of radii instead of areas. 8 N divides by the area ratio. 200 N assumes force, not pressure, is transmitted.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Pascal's law and its applications

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A soap bubble has a radius of 2 cm. The surface tension of the soap solution is 0.03 N/m. The excess pressure inside the bubble over the outside pressure is:

solution.concept: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble
solution.explanation: A soap bubble has two surfaces (inner and outer), so its excess pressure is twice that of a liquid drop: ΔP = 4S/r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 Pa uses 2S/r, which is for a liquid drop with one surface. 1.5 Pa uses S/r. 12 Pa takes 2 cm as the diameter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', excess pressure across a curved surface

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: According to Stokes' law, the viscous drag force on a small sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of coefficient of viscosity η is proportional to:

solution.concept: Stokes' law
solution.explanation: For a small sphere moving slowly (streamline flow around it), F = 6πηrv: the drag is proportional to the first power of each of η, r and v.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong option raises one of the three quantities to the second power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Stokes' law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (physical quantity) with List-II (its SI unit).

List-I:
A. Surface tension
B. Coefficient of viscosity
C. Young's modulus
D. Thermal conductivity

List-II:
I. W m⁻¹ K⁻¹
II. N m⁻¹
III. N m⁻²
IV. N s m⁻²

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: SI units from defining equations
solution.explanation: Write each quantity from its defining equation and read off the unit.
steps: Surface tension = force/length → N m⁻¹ → II
Viscosity: F = ηA(dv/dx) → η in N s m⁻² (Pa s) → IV
Young's modulus = stress/strain → N m⁻² (Pa) → III
Thermal conductivity: H = KA ΔT/L → W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The usual slips swap surface tension (force per length) with modulus (force per area), or viscosity with modulus (they differ by a factor of time).
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 500 W electric heater immersed in 1 kg of a liquid raises its temperature from 20 °C to 45 °C in 2 minutes. Assuming no heat is lost, the specific heat capacity of the liquid is:

solution.concept: Calorimetry: Q = mcΔT
solution.explanation: All the electrical energy supplied, P × t, heats the liquid.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 leaves the time in minutes. 1333 divides by the final temperature (45) instead of the rise. 3000 divides by the initial temperature (20).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe. At a wide section its speed is 2 m/s and at a narrow section it is 4 m/s. Taking the density of water as 1000 kg/m³, the pressure at the wide section exceeds that at the narrow section by:

solution.concept: Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe
solution.explanation: With no change in height, P + ½ρv² is constant along a streamline. Where the fluid moves faster, the pressure is lower.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2000 Pa squares the difference of speeds instead of taking the difference of squares. 8000 Pa uses only the faster speed. 12000 Pa drops the ½.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Water rises in a clean glass capillary tube dipped in it, while mercury is depressed in a glass capillary tube.
Statement II: The angle of contact between mercury and glass is obtuse.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Capillarity and angle of contact
solution.explanation: Capillary rise h = 2S cos θ/(rρg). For water on clean glass θ is acute (cos θ > 0), so water rises. For mercury on glass θ is obtuse (about 140°, cos θ < 0), so mercury is depressed. Both statements are true.
steps: Statement I true, Statement II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', angle of contact and capillary rise
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Eight identical small raindrops, each falling through air with terminal velocity v, combine to form one bigger drop. Assuming Stokes' law holds, the terminal velocity of the bigger drop is:

solution.concept: Terminal velocity v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η ∝ r²
solution.explanation: The volume is conserved when the drops merge, so the radius of the big drop follows from R³ = 8r³. Terminal velocity then scales as the square of the radius.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2v assumes v_t ∝ r. 8v assumes v_t ∝ volume. v assumes terminal velocity does not depend on size.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At room temperature, a metal object feels colder to the touch than a wooden object kept at the same temperature.
Reason (R): Metals have a much higher thermal conductivity than wood, so they conduct heat away from the hand much faster.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Thermal conductivity
solution.explanation: Both objects are at the same temperature, below body temperature. The sensation of cold depends on how fast heat leaves the skin. Metal conducts heat away from the hand quickly; wood, a poor conductor, does not. R is true and explains A.
steps: Same temperature, but different rates of heat flow from the hand
K_metal ≫ K_wood → faster heat loss → feels colder
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', conduction
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Young's modulus is defined for liquids as well as for solids.
Statement II: Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Moduli of elasticity and Hooke's law
solution.explanation: Young's modulus involves a change in length of a body with a definite shape, so it applies only to solids. Liquids (and gases) have only a bulk modulus. Statement I is false. Statement II is Hooke's law: true.
steps: Liquids have no definite length or shape → no Young's modulus → I false
Hooke's law: stress ∝ strain within the elastic limit → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Hooke's law and elastic moduli
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: 50 g of ice at 0 °C is dropped into 200 g of water at 40 °C in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. Take the specific heat of water as 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ and the latent heat of fusion of ice as 80 cal g⁻¹. The final temperature of the mixture is:

solution.concept: Calorimetry with a change of state
solution.explanation: First check whether all the ice can melt. Then the remaining heat warms the whole 250 g of water.
steps: Heat the water can give in cooling to 0 °C: 200 × 1 × 40 = 8000 cal
Heat to melt all the ice: 50 × 80 = 4000 cal < 8000 cal → all the ice melts
Heat left = 4000 cal, shared by 250 g: ΔT = 4000/250 = 16 °C
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 °C ignores the latent heat of fusion. 0 °C assumes some ice is left, but 8000 cal is more than enough to melt it all. 20 °C forgets that the 50 g of melted ice must also be warmed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', calorimetry and change of state

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wide open tank stands on level ground and is filled with water to a height of 5.0 m above the ground. A small hole is made in its side wall at a height of 3.2 m above the ground. Taking g = 10 m/s², the water jet strikes the ground at a horizontal distance from the wall of:

solution.concept: Torricelli's law followed by horizontal projection
solution.explanation: The speed of efflux depends on the depth of the hole below the water surface (Torricelli). The jet then falls freely through the height of the hole above the ground.
steps: Depth of hole below surface = 5.0 − 3.2 = 1.8 m
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.0 m uses the full water height (5 m) for the efflux speed. 3.4 m uses v = √(gh), missing the 2. 6.4 m uses the hole's height (3.2 m) as its depth below the surface.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', speed of efflux: Torricelli's law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two rods P and Q of the same cross-sectional area are joined end to end. Rod P has thermal conductivity K and length L; rod Q has thermal conductivity 3K and length 2L. The free end of P is kept at 100 °C and the free end of Q at 0 °C. The sides are insulated. In the steady state, the temperature of the junction is:

solution.concept: Steady-state conduction through rods in series
solution.explanation: In the steady state the same heat current flows through both rods: H = KA ΔT/L for each.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 °C attaches the rods the other way round. 25 °C ignores the different lengths. 50 °C ignores both the conductivities and the lengths.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', conduction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about fluids are correct?

(a) In steady (streamline) flow, the velocity of the fluid at any given point does not change with time.
(b) Bernoulli's principle expresses the conservation of energy for the steady flow of an incompressible, non-viscous fluid.
(c) The viscosity of a gas increases as its temperature rises.
(d) The surface tension of a liquid generally decreases as its temperature rises.
(e) Pascal's law states that a pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished only in the direction of the applied force.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Streamline flow, Bernoulli, viscosity, surface tension and Pascal's law
solution.explanation: In steady flow each point has a fixed velocity. Bernoulli's equation is the work-energy theorem for an ideal fluid. The viscosity of liquids falls with temperature but that of gases rises. Surface tension falls as temperature rises. Pascal's law says the pressure is transmitted equally in all directions.
steps: (c) True: gases become more viscous when heated (liquids less)
(e) False: transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the container walls
solution.why_others_wrong: (a), (b) and (d) only leaves out (c), the gas-viscosity trap. Every other option includes the false (e) or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', streamline flow, Bernoulli's principle, viscosity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A liquid drop of radius R breaks up isothermally into 1000 identical droplets. If S is the surface tension of the liquid, the work done in this process is:

solution.concept: Surface energy: work = S × increase in surface area
solution.explanation: The total volume stays the same, so each droplet has radius r = R/10. The work needed equals S times the increase in total surface area.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40πR²S uses the final area and forgets to subtract the initial area. 72πR²S counts two surfaces per drop, as for a soap bubble. 9πR²S uses πR² instead of 4πR² for the area of a sphere.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', surface energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. The change in its internal energy is:

solution.concept: First law of thermodynamics: ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW
solution.explanation: Heat supplied to the system goes partly into raising its internal energy and partly into work done by it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 700 J adds the work instead of subtracting it. −300 J gets the sign convention backwards. 200 J is the work done, not the change in internal energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The zeroth law of thermodynamics leads directly to the concept of:

solution.concept: Zeroth law and thermal equilibrium
solution.explanation: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. The physical quantity that has the same value for systems in thermal equilibrium is temperature.
steps: A ~ C and B ~ C (thermal equilibrium) → A ~ B
The common property of systems in equilibrium = temperature
solution.why_others_wrong: Internal energy comes from the first law, and entropy from the second. Heat capacity is a property of a body, not the quantity the zeroth law defines.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', zeroth law of thermodynamics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When an ideal gas undergoes an isothermal process, the change in its internal energy is zero.
Statement II: In an adiabatic process, no heat is exchanged between the system and its surroundings.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Isothermal and adiabatic processes
solution.explanation: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so at constant temperature ΔU = 0: Statement I is true. An adiabatic process is defined by ΔQ = 0: Statement II is true.
steps: Ideal gas: U = U(T) → isothermal → ΔU = 0 → I true
Adiabatic: ΔQ = 0 by definition → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', thermodynamic processes
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two moles of an ideal gas at 300 K expand isothermally and reversibly until the volume doubles. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and ln 2 = 0.693, the work done by the gas is about:

solution.concept: Work in a reversible isothermal process
solution.explanation: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, W = ∫P dV = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.98 kJ leaves out the ln 2 factor (it is nRT). 1.73 kJ uses n = 1. 1.50 kJ uses log₁₀ 2 = 0.301 instead of ln 2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', isothermal process

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) at 300 K is compressed adiabatically and reversibly to one-eighth of its initial volume. Its final temperature is:

solution.concept: Adiabatic relation TV^(γ−1) = constant
solution.explanation: In a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas, T V^(γ−1) stays constant. Here γ − 1 = 2/3.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2400 K uses T ∝ 1/V (power 1). 600 K uses the power 1/3. 9600 K uses the power γ = 5/3, which belongs to PV^γ, not TV^(γ−1).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', adiabatic process

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The work done by a gas in going from one equilibrium state to another depends on the path followed.
Reason (R): The internal energy of an ideal gas is a state function.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Path functions and state functions
solution.explanation: Work is the area under the P–V curve, which differs from path to path, so A is true. Internal energy depends only on the state, so R is true. But R does not explain A: it is about internal energy, while A is about work. The path dependence of work is due to the different areas under different P–V curves.
steps: W = ∫P dV = area under the path → path-dependent → A true
U depends only on the state → R true
R is about U, not W → R does not explain A
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A is the trap: R is true, but a property of U cannot explain why W depends on the path.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', heat, internal energy and work; state variables
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal diatomic gas (Cv = 5R/2) is heated at constant pressure. The fraction of the heat supplied that is used in doing external work is:

solution.concept: First law at constant pressure
solution.explanation: At constant pressure, Q = nC_pΔT, ΔU = nC_vΔT and W = PΔV = nRΔT. So W/Q = R/C_p.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5/7 is the fraction that goes into internal energy. 2/5 divides by C_v instead of C_p. 1 is true only for an isothermal process of an ideal gas, where ΔU = 0.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal gas is taken round the cycle A → B → C → D → A.
